name: Karl Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a maintenance crew in the forest hills above Lindvik, which means trees, mostly. Trees falling on lines, trees growing into lines, and a storm every few weeks in winter that knocks out half the valley. I'm a second-year apprentice, so I'm the one on the ground rigging the ropes, feeding the chipper, digging out a rotten pole, and fetching whatever the climber shouts for. We go out from the depot at seven and in a storm we can be out for eighteen hours. I like working with my hands outdoors, and I like the old-timers on the crew, who don't waste words. What wears me out is the long storm shifts and how slow I am with the electrical theory.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You came to this late. What were you doing before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty years as a carpenter, my own small business, kitchens and roofs and decks. In 2023 I hurt my back, and the same year a builder went bust owing me eleven thousand, and that was the end of it. The power company was taking older apprentices, and I liked the idea of learning a proper trade again from the bottom. My wife Inge works in the kitchen at the primary school, and between us we get by, but there's no savings left after the business went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, people always get carried away with new gadgets. At the depot I'd say a computer never fixed a fallen line. At church I wouldn't say much, it's not that kind of place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes. I'd keep learning the trade, keep my head down, and get my qualification. Honestly I'd be glad, because I've had enough upheaval for one lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the apprenticeship, aim to qualify by 2028, and take every storm shift for the overtime. On weekends I'd keep doing a bit of carpentry for neighbours, cash jobs, a new gate here, a shelf there. Slowly, I'd try to build a month's savings back up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really. I've got enough to think about without robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned using AI now and then. When do you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son-in-law showed me how to have it write up a quote for a carpentry job, all neat with the costs listed. I use it for that, and once in a while to explain something from the electrical theory book. But I always check with Nils, the old foreman, because a mistake on a line is a funeral, not a bad shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a month's savings mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean I could sleep through a storm warning without thinking about what happens if I'm hurt. When the business went, we cashed in everything, even Inge's little savings account from her mother. I'd like to put that back for her, that's a matter of pride.

S0.say: He's not surprised, because people always get carried away with gadgets. At the depot he'd say a computer never fixed a fallen line.
S0.think: Nothing changes for him: he keeps learning the trade and working toward his qualification. He'd be glad, having had enough upheaval for one lifetime.
S0.do: Keeps going with his apprenticeship, aims to qualify by 2028 and takes every storm shift for overtime. Does weekend cash carpentry for neighbours and slowly rebuilds a month of savings.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved to have one less thing to think about.
S0.quote: But I always check with Nils, the old foreman, because a mistake on a line is a funeral, not a bad shelf.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is a former self-employed carpenter who lost his business to a back injury and a bad debt. He uses AI occasionally and practically, but defers to experienced colleagues on safety. Rebuilding his wife's savings is a matter of personal pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get on with it and adapt, like folks always have. At the depot I'd tell the young ones that a good trade will still see them right. I'd say the government should help with apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think line work in the forest is safe for a good while. A robot isn't going to climb a wet slope in the dark with a chainsaw. The paperwork might change, and that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the apprenticeship and learn the new tools once Nils and the others are using them. I'd keep the carpentry going on weekends. I'd maybe look at whether there's a market for wooden things people still want made by hand, because I think there will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd feel like I'd picked the right trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships, not handouts. What's the difference to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprenticeship gives a man something to stand on. A handout gives him something to lean on, and leaning gets to be a habit. I'd rather the money went to teaching people trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You also said wooden things made by hand. What do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chopping boards, small benches, toys for grandkids. When everything's made by machine, I reckon some people will pay a bit extra for a thing a person made. I've already sold a few at the church fair.

S1.say: People need to adapt, as they always have, and a good trade will still see them right. The government should fund apprenticeships, not handouts.
S1.think: He believes forest line work is safe for a good while, since robots won't climb wet slopes in the dark with chainsaws. Paperwork changes would suit him fine.
S1.do: Keeps at his apprenticeship and learns new tools once experienced colleagues use them. Keeps up weekend carpentry and explores selling handmade wooden goods.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, feeling he picked the right trade.
S1.quote: An apprenticeship gives a man something to stand on. A handout gives him something to lean on, and leaning gets to be a habit.
S1.fieldNote: Karl's traditional views come through clearly: apprenticeships over handouts, hard work over government help. He is open to new tools once proven by others. His idea of selling handmade goods reflects a belief that people will value human craft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and nobody voted for it. At the depot I'd say we need to stick together and look after each other. I'd want the government to slow it down, but I wouldn't hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty, barely qualified. If robots can climb poles by 2028, I've got nothing: no savings, no business, a bad back. That's the honest truth of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard: no new tools, sell the old van I use for carpentry and keep the car. I'd make as much as I could from carpentry while people still want it. And I'd ask our son, the plumber, if he could take me on as a helper, though he might be in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. I don't say that often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask your son for work. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Upside down. I taught him to hold a hammer, and now I'd be asking him for a job. But that's what family is for, and I'd rather that than a government office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did the two years of warning help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. It gives me time to sell what I don't need and maybe finish my qualification. But two years for a man of fifty-eight with nothing in the bank is like being told the storm is two hours away; you can tie down the shed, but you can't move the house.

S2.say: It's too fast and nobody voted for it. He would urge his crew to stick together and want the government to slow it down, without much hope.
S2.think: At sixty and barely qualified, with no savings, no business and a bad back, robots climbing poles would leave him with nothing.
S2.do: Cuts back hard, selling his old carpentry van, and earns what he can from carpentry while demand lasts. Asks his plumber son to take him on as a helper.
S2.feel: Scared, which he admits doesn't happen often.
S2.quote: Like being told the storm is two hours away; you can tie down the shed, but you can't move the house.
S2.fieldNote: Karl admits real fear in the fast scenario, which is unusual for him. He would turn to family, specifically his son, before any government help, despite the awkwardness. The storm comparison captured his sense of having almost no room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is better, a man can plan in five years. At the depot I'd say get qualified and get ready. I'd still want the government to put money into apprenticeships for the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three, qualified by then. I might make it to retirement on the lines, or at least close. I'd still worry about money, but less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by 2028 and put every spare bit of overtime into savings, maybe a hundred a month. I'd build up the carpentry on the side into something steady, maybe a stall at the market once a month. I'd talk to Inge about what we could cut if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Like a long storm shift, you just keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Inge say about cutting back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we've been cutting back since 2023, Karl, what's left? And she'd be right. Maybe the car, maybe the holiday to her sister's every summer, but that would break her heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young apprentices on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get their tickets and learn the new machines as well as the old. I'd tell them to save, because I didn't, and look where it got me. A trade is a good thing, but a trade and some money in the bank is better.

S3.say: Five years is better, because a man can plan in five years. He would tell crewmates to get qualified and want government money for apprenticeships in new jobs.
S3.think: At sixty-three and qualified, he might reach retirement on the lines or close to it. He'd still worry about money, but less.
S3.do: Qualifies by 2028 and saves about a hundred a month from overtime. Builds his carpentry into a steady sideline with a monthly market stall and talks to his wife about possible cuts.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, like keeping going through a long storm shift.
S3.quote: A trade is a good thing, but a trade and some money in the bank is better.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Karl can plan a path to qualification and possibly retirement. He is honest that past cutbacks leave little room. His advice to young apprentices reflects his own regret about not saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair, there's no excuse for anyone not being ready. At the depot I'd tell the young ones to plan now. I'd say families and communities need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so I'd be retired or close. I never planned on stopping work entirely anyway; I'll be making benches till I drop. It doesn't feel like much of a threat to me personally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, keep working on the lines, and keep the carpentry going. I'd save a bit every month for Inge. I'd tell our grandchildren to learn a trade and to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sad for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said benches till you drop. Is that a plan or a joke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. My father worked until his hands shook, and I'll probably be the same. A man needs work, and if no one needs me on the lines, I'll make something useful in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you sad for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandson, Leo, who's sixteen and thinks he'll be a mechanic. In ten years maybe there are no mechanics. I'd tell him to learn to fix the robots, and to make things with his hands as well, because people will always want something real.

S4.say: Ten years is fair, so there's no excuse for anyone not being ready. He would tell younger workers to plan now and say families and communities should look after each other.
S4.think: At sixty-eight he would be retired or close, and he never planned to stop working entirely anyway. It doesn't feel like much of a threat to him personally.
S4.do: Qualifies, keeps working on the lines and keeps up his carpentry. Saves a little each month for his wife and tells his grandchildren to learn a trade and save.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some sadness for young people.
S4.quote: A man needs work, and if no one needs me on the lines, I'll make something useful in the shed.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Karl is calm, partly because he never expected to stop working. His sadness is for his grandson, whose chosen trade may vanish. He sees human craft as something that will still matter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have only just qualified, with no savings and a bad back. What would help is apprenticeships and paid training for the new jobs, and a way for older workers to stay on till retirement. I don't want charity; I want a chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. A man my age starting over as an apprentice takes a lot of swallowing. But I'd rather be the oldest apprentice on the crew than the youngest man on the sofa.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the oldest apprentice on the crew than the youngest man on the sofa.
portrait: Karl Hansen is a 58-year-old second-year apprentice on a forest maintenance crew above Lindvik, who took up line work after his carpentry business ended in 2023 with a back injury and an unpaid debt. He and his wife Inge, a school kitchen worker, have no savings left, and he does weekend carpentry for cash. He uses AI now and then for quotes and theory but always checks with his foreman. He believes in apprenticeships over handouts and stays calm in the milder pictures, is scared in the 2028 picture and would turn to his son for work. With ten years he expects to keep working with his hands in some form.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because he would have only just qualified, with no savings and a bad back.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and paid training for new jobs, and a way for older workers to stay on until retirement; he wants a chance to work, not charity.
